name: Thomas Hobbes
summary: Hobbes argued that life without a sovereign is a war of all against all, so people covenant to give one undivided, absolute power the right to make law, judge, tax and command the army and doctrine. He held that subjects may not resist or divide that power, preferred monarchy with a hereditary succession chosen by the ruler, and put the church under the civil sovereign.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 gives the sovereign the right to levy money and soldiers as he judges necessary, and Behemoth treats the Petition of Right, which ended the king's power to levy money without consent, as a surrender of essential sovereign power.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Leviathan ch. 30 says those unable to work must not be left to private charity but be provided for by the laws of the commonwealth.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Leviathan ch. 42 has pastors, bishops included, hold their office by the civil sovereign's authority, not by their own right to govern the church.

clerical-rule.rationale: Leviathan ch. 29 and 42 argue that a ghostly power claiming supremacy over the civil sovereign dissolves the commonwealth.

conscription.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 and 30 give the sovereign the right to levy soldiers when he judges it necessary, and ch. 21 says that when defence needs all able to bear arms, every one is obliged.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Leviathan ch. 17-18 founds sovereignty on the covenant of every man with every man, and ch. 20 on the consent of the vanquished, not on victory itself.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: In A Dialogue of the Common Law the Philosopher sees no harm to the commonwealth in courts that decide by witnesses without juries, and holds the king's judges, not custom, give the law its force.

death-penalty.rationale: Leviathan ch. 21 and 28 hold that the sovereign has the power of life and death over subjects, with capital punishment among the punishments he may impose.

democracy-best.rationale: Leviathan ch. 19 compares the three forms and finds monarchy more convenient for peace than a sovereign assembly; the form matters by aptitude, not by who rules.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Leviathan ch. 19 says leaving the succession to a new choice dissolves the commonwealth, against the intention of those who instituted it.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Leviathan ch. 19 has the sovereign dispose of the succession and presumes, absent a will, that his own child is preferred to any other.

elective-rulers.rationale: Leviathan ch. 19 says if the succession is left to a new choice the commonwealth is dissolved and power goes to whoever can seize it.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 makes the sovereign judge of what is necessary for peace and defence, and does whatever he thinks needed to prevent discord at home.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 and 26 hold that nothing the sovereign does to a subject can be injustice and that he is not bound by the civil laws.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Leviathan ch. 15 makes acknowledging each man as equal by nature a law of nature, and ch. 30 requires equal justice for rich and poor, great and small.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Leviathan ch. 21 defines liberty as the absence of external impediments, which fits subjects of absolute sovereigns; democratic liberty is no greater than under a monarch.

freedom-is-self-government-of-desire.rationale: Leviathan ch. 21 defines a free man as one who is not hindered in doing what he has the will to do.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 says command of the militia belongs to the sovereign, so he is always generalissimo.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: Leviathan ch. 26 argues a parliament is not sovereign where someone else can assemble or dissolve it, which is how he reads the English king.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Leviathan ch. 24 says that without a commonwealth whatever a man gets and keeps by force is neither property nor community but uncertainty; property comes only from the sovereign's law.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: De Cive ch. 8 says dominion over beasts comes from the right of nature, so a man may tame or kill them as he sees fit.

initiating-nondefensive-force-unjustifie.rationale: Leviathan ch. 13 holds that anticipation, striking first by force or craft, is the most reasonable way to secure oneself against others.

legal-duty-to-work.rationale: Leviathan ch. 30 says able-bodied poor "are to be forced to work", with laws to encourage trades so they cannot plead lack of employment.

member-state-blocks-federal-overreach.rationale: Leviathan ch. 29 calls dividing the sovereign power a disease and holds that a body able to check the sovereign makes two sovereigns.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: Leviathan ch. 24 counts just war among the ways of obtaining foreign commodities and ch. 30 names war as the last remedy for an over-peopled world.

minority-veto.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 says a man who dissented from the majority's choice of sovereign must consent with the rest or be justly destroyed.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Leviathan ch. 29 ("Mixt Government") says a government mixing monarchy, aristocracy and democracy is no government but three factions.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Leviathan ch. 14 and 21 make defending one's own body, even against the sovereign's sword, an inalienable right of nature.

night-watchman-state.rationale: De Cive ch. 13 says the sovereign's duty, the people's safety, includes every benefit of life, not bare protection, and he must also instruct, encourage trades and relieve the poor.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Leviathan ch. 22 calls chartered merchant companies monopolies that are ill for the people at home, and says they would be fine only if left free to trade at home.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Leviathan ch. 26 says the civil law binds by the covenant of subjection, and the law of nature requires keeping covenants.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Leviathan ch. 26 says a parliament is supreme only where it holds sovereignty and cannot be dissolved by others; in England he treats the king in parliament as the controller of laws.

party-controls-media.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 gives the sovereign the right to judge which doctrines may be taught and to examine all books before publication.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Leviathan ch. 19 says those who bear the people's person, in whatever form, prefer their private good over the public one when the two cross.

positive-liberty.rationale: Leviathan ch. 14 and 21 define liberty as absence of external impediment to motion, not as having the means to act.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 annexes all judicature to the sovereign power; without it, men would return to protecting themselves by private strength.

property-fundamental.rationale: Leviathan ch. 29 lists the doctrine that subjects hold absolute property excluding the sovereign as a cause of dissolution; ch. 24 makes property an act of the sovereign power, which can redistribute it.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Leviathan ch. 24 has the sovereign distribute land and set the rules of property by what he judges agreeable to equity and the common good.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Leviathan ch. 29 condemns the doctrine that each subject judges good and evil by private conscience instead of the civil law.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: Leviathan ch. 30 says surplus poor transplanted to thinly peopled lands are not to exterminate those they find but to constrain them to live closer together.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 holds that subjects cannot lawfully depose a sovereign or pretend a breach of covenant, because he makes no covenant with them.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 says subjects cannot change the form of government or be freed by pretended forfeiture, and ch. 29 blames seditious doctrines for dissolutions.

separate-church-state.rationale: Leviathan ch. 29 and 42 call a separate ghostly power a kingdom divided in itself and make the civil sovereign supreme pastor of his subjects.

separated-powers.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 and 29 call dividing the sovereign power (force and justice, or legislative and executive) a doctrine against the essence of a commonwealth.

single-common-good.rationale: De Cive ch. 13 tells rulers to regard the common benefit of many, not any private interest, and to keep down ambition and break factions.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 forbids subjects to change the form of government they instituted and treats attempts to depose the sovereign as unjust.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Leviathan ch. 21 says a man who has enrolled as a soldier or taken pay must fight and may not run, except for timorous nature before enlisting.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Leviathan ch. 26 says the sovereign is not subject to the civil laws he makes and may free himself from them when he pleases.

state-harmful.rationale: Leviathan ch. 13 and 17 describe life without a sovereign as a war of every man against every man and make the commonwealth the only escape from it.

strong-leader.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18-19 argues sovereign power must be undivided and absolute so that no rival body can block it, and ch. 19 judges monarchy the most convenient form.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Leviathan ch. 42 says every Christian sovereign is supreme pastor and all other pastors derive their right to teach from him.

surveillance-ok.rationale: De Cive ch. 13 argues rulers need spies to discover the counsels of those who may harm the state, as necessary for its defence.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Leviathan ch. 30 says equal taxation depends not on equality of riches but on what each consumes, and prefers taxes on consumption.

taxation-theft.rationale: Leviathan ch. 30 calls taxes the wages due to those who hold the public sword to protect each man's trade and calling, so they are a debt owed, not theft.

universal-morality.rationale: Leviathan ch. 15 says the laws of nature are immutable and eternal: injustice, ingratitude and pride can never be made lawful.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Leviathan ch. 18 and 21 say nothing the sovereign commands can be injustice to a subject, because every subject authorised his acts.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Leviathan ch. 30 provides by law for the impotent but says the strong-bodied are to be forced to work.
